docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
Common Patterns for Solving String DSA Problems String problems often involve manipulation, searching, or transformation. The following patterns are frequently used to solve them:

  1. Two-Pointer Technique
  2. Sliding Window
  3. Hash Map / Frequency Counting
  4. String Reversal
  5. Pattern Matching (e.g., KMP, Rabin-Karp)
  6. Palindrome Checking
  7. String Transformation / Parsing
  8. Anagram Grouping
  9. Dynamic Programming (for complex string problems)
  10. Stack for Parentheses or Matching

I'll demonstrate each pattern with a sample problem and JavaScript solution, focusing on string-specific applications.

docs.title: 🎯 Beginner Roadmap: Focus on These 4 Patterns First
docs.text:
These 4 patterns are used not just in string problems, but across many types of problems in JavaScript and general DSA (Data Structures & Algorithms).

Let’s walk through each one and see where else it applies — beyond strings.

docs.title: ✅ 1. Sliding Window
docs.text:
[Sliding Window]
            ↙      ↘
       [Strings]  [Arrays]
         ↙             ↘
  Longest Substring    Max Sum Subarray (Size K)
  Without Repeats      Longest Subarray w/ Sum < K

🔄 Used In:

  • Strings: Substrings, anagrams, distinct characters
  • Arrays: Subarrays with sum ≤ K, max average, product, etc.
💡 Example (Arrays)
// Max sum of a subarray of size k
function maxSum(nums, k) {
  let sum = 0,
    max = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += nums[i];
  max = sum;

  for (let i = k; i < nums.length; i++) {
    sum += nums[i] - nums[i - k];
    max = Math.max(max, sum);
  }

  return max;
}

docs.title: ✅ 2. Two Pointers
docs.text:
[Two Pointers]
           ↙     ↘
     [Strings]  [Arrays]
       ↙           ↘
  Palindromes     Sorted 2-Sum / Remove Duplicates

🔄 Used In:

  • Strings: Palindromes, reverse, compare
  • Arrays: Sorted array problems (e.g., 2-sum, remove duplicates)
  • Linked Lists: Detect cycle, reverse list, middle of list
💡 Example (Arrays)
// Two Sum (sorted array)
function twoSum(numbers, target) {
  let left = 0,
    right = numbers.length - 1;

  while (left < right) {
    const sum = numbers[left] + numbers[right];
    if (sum === target) return [left + 1, right + 1];
    else if (sum < target) left++;
    else right--;
  }
}

docs.title: ✅ 3. Hash Map / Frequency Counter
docs.text:
[Hash Map / Frequency Counter]
           ↙         ↘
       [Strings]   [Arrays/General]
         ↙               ↘
    Anagram Checks     Find Duplicates / Frequency Sort

🔄 Used In:

  • Strings: Anagram, character count, duplicates
  • Arrays: Find duplicates, frequency of elements
  • Graphs / Trees: Adjacency lists, visited nodes, memoization
💡 Example (Arrays)
// Find first duplicate element
function findDuplicate(arr) {
  const map = new Map();

  for (let num of arr) {
    if (map.has(num)) return num;
    map.set(num, 1);
  }

  return -1;
}

docs.title: ✅ 4. Stack for Strings
docs.text:
[Stack]
              ↙   ↘
        [Strings] [Arrays]
           ↙          ↘
  Valid Parentheses  Next Greater Element

🔄 Used In:

  • Strings: Valid parentheses, decoding
  • Arrays: Next greater element, histogram max area
  • Trees: Iterative DFS traversal
  • General: Undo operations, parsing expressions
💡 Example (Arrays)
// Next Greater Element
function nextGreater(nums) {
  let stack = [],
    result = Array(nums.length).fill(-1);

  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    while (stack.length && nums[i] > nums[stack[stack.length - 1]]) {
      let index = stack.pop();
      result[index] = nums[i];
    }
    stack.push(i);
  }

  return result;
}

docs.text: Step Pattern Example Problem Why Important 1️⃣ Sliding Window Longest substring without repeats High-frequency interview topic 2️⃣ Two Pointers Valid Palindrome Simple logic + good pointer practice 3️⃣ Hash Map Valid Anagram Teaches frequency counting 4️⃣ Stack Valid Parentheses, Remove Duplicates Builds understanding of parsing logic

docs.title: 🧪 Frontend System Design Prompt (Banking Project)
docs.text:
📝 Prompt:

"Design the frontend architecture for a web banking application used by millions of users. The app includes features like viewing account balances, transferring money, transaction history, user settings, and support chat."

docs.title: 🧠 Step-by-Step: How to Think Like an Architect
✅ 1. Requirements Clarification (Always Start Here)
docs.text:
Ask clarifying questions:

  • Users: Retail customers only? Or include business accounts?
  • Devices: Web + mobile web? Responsive?
  • Data freshness: Do balances update in real-time?
  • Security: How strict is the session/token handling?
  • Scale: Millions of users? Any internationalization?
  • Feature scope: MVP or long-term design?

docs.title: 🧱 2. High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
Banking Web App
├── Auth Layer (SSO, MFA, token refresh)
├── Core Layout (NavBar, Sidebar, Footer)
├── Modules
│   ├── Accounts
│   ├── Transactions
│   ├── Transfers
│   ├── Settings
│   └── Support (chat, helpdesk)

Use a feature-based folder structure:

/src
  /features
    /accounts
    /transactions
    /transfers
    /settings
    /support
  /components
    /ui
    /layout
  /lib
  /hooks
  /services
  /state
  /types
  /pages (if using Next.js)

docs.title: 🧠 3. Key Architectural Considerations
docs.text:
🔐 Authentication & Authorization

  • Use JWT or session cookies (secure, HTTP-only)
  • Multi-factor auth (MFA) integration
  • Role-based access control (RBAC) on frontend routes + UI

🧾 State Management

Type Tool Server state React Query (TanStack Query) Client state Zustand / Redux Toolkit Form state React Hook Form + Zod/Yup
  • Use query caching to minimize balance fetches
  • Use React Query for transactions, with pagination + prefetching

🧩 Component Architecture

  • Atomic design or headless components
  • Shared design tokens (spacing, color, typography)
  • Accessible UI (ARIA, keyboard nav, screen reader)

🧪 Testing Strategy

  • Jest for unit tests
  • React Testing Library for component tests
  • Cypress or Playwright for E2E testing

Test scenarios:

  • Token expiry
  • Large transaction list
  • Concurrent transfer edge cases

🌍 Internationalization (i18n)

  • Currency, language, locale formatting
  • Use i18next or react-intl

🧰 Error & Logging

  • Use Error Boundaries
  • Connect to Sentry for error tracking
  • Fallback UIs for network/API errors

docs.title: 🚀 4. Performance & Scalability
docs.text: Concern Strategy Bundle size Code splitting with dynamic imports Large data sets Virtualize long lists (e.g., react-window) API optimization Pagination, optimistic updates, background refetch Rendering SSR/CSR with Next.js (Next 13 app router) Caching HTTP + React Query + CDN for static assets

docs.title: ⚙️ 5. DevOps & CI/CD Considerations
docs.text:
• Linting, Prettier, and TypeScript strict mode
  • GitHub Actions / GitLab CI
  • Feature flags for rolling out features (LaunchDarkly or homegrown)
  • Lighthouse CI to catch regressions
  • End-to-end monitoring

docs.title: 🔒 6. Security First (Critical for Banking)
docs.text:
• Sanitize all inputs (forms, chat)

  • Use Content Security Policy (CSP)

  • Prevent:

    • XSS
    • CSRF (use proper tokens)
    • Clickjacking (use frame options headers)

  • Set up proper error logging without leaking sensitive data

docs.title: 🧠 7. Think Like a Team Lead
docs.text:
• Separate modules for each major feature (accounts, transfers, etc.)
  • Define shared interfaces and contracts between features
  • Document component APIs and expected behaviors
  • Use a design system to unify look/feel across modules
  • Consider monorepo if building multiple apps (e.g., admin portal, customer app)

docs.title: 🏁 TL;DR – Final Output Summary
docs.text: Area Your Choices Folder Structure Feature-based (scalable) State Management React Query + Zustand/Redux Component Architecture Headless + atomic + accessible Performance Code-splitting, caching, virtualization Testing Jest + RTL + Cypress Auth JWT + MFA + RBAC DevOps CI/CD, feature flags, monitoring Security XSS/CSRF/CSP + error sanitization Design System Custom tokens + Storybook Team Scaling Shared contracts, documentation, module separation

3. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters

Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without duplicate characters.

Example 1
Input: s = "abcabcbb"
Output: 3
Explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.
Example 2
Input: s = "bbbbb"
Output: 1
Explanation: The answer is "b", with the length of 1.
Example 3
Input: s = "pwwkew"
Output: 3
Explanation: The answer is "wke", with the length of 3.
Notice that the answer must be a substring, "pwke" is a subsequence and not a substring.

Constraints:

  • 0 <= s.length <= 5 * 10 square 4
  • s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
/**
 * @param {string} s
 * @return {number}
 */

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: • Leetcode Problem String

docs.title: Technique
docs.text: When tackling JavaScript string-based DSA (Data Structures & Algorithms) questions, certain patterns and techniques show up repeatedly. These patterns are not specific to JavaScript but apply well to JS because of its string methods, hash maps (objects/Map), and functional tools.

docs.title: Common Patterns & Techniques for Solving JS String DSA Questions
docs.text: Here’s a breakdown of the most important ones:

docs.title: 1. Sliding Window
docs.text:
Used when you're working with substrings, windows of characters, or consecutive elements.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Longest substring without repeating characters
  • Minimum/maximum window substring
  • Anagrams in a string

Key Idea: Use two pointers (left and right) to maintain a window.

// Example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
let set = new Set();
let left = 0;
let maxLen = 0;

for (let right = 0; right < s.length; right++) {
  while (set.has(s[right])) {
    set.delete(s[left]);
    left++;
  }
  set.add(s[right]);
  maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, right - left + 1);
}

docs.title: 2. Two Pointers
docs.text:
Used when comparing parts of a string, palindromes, or doing in-place operations.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Valid palindrome
  • Reverse a string
  • Compare characters from both ends
// Example: Valid Palindrome
let left = 0;
let right = s.length - 1;

while (left < right) {
  if (s[left] !== s[right]) return false;
  left++;
  right--;
}
return true;

docs.title: 3. Hash Map / Frequency Counter
docs.text:
Used to count character occurrences, detect duplicates, or track frequencies.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Anagram check
  • Longest substring with at most K distinct characters
  • Character replacement
// Example: Check if two strings are anagrams
function isAnagram(s, t) {
  if (s.length !== t.length) return false;
  const count = {};

  for (let char of s) {
    count[char] = (count[char] || 0) + 1;
  }

  for (let char of t) {
    if (!count[char]) return false;
    count[char]--;
  }

  return true;
}

docs.title: 4. Stack-Based Processing
docs.text:
Used for balanced parentheses, decoding strings, or processing backspaces.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Valid parentheses
  • Decode string like "3[a2[c]]" → "accaccacc"
  • Backspace string compare
// Example: Valid Parentheses
let stack = [];

for (let char of s) {
  if (char === "(") stack.push(char);
  else if (char === ")") {
    if (stack.length === 0) return false;
    stack.pop();
  }
}
return stack.length === 0;

docs.title: 5. Expand Around Center (Palindrome)
docs.text:
Used for palindromic substrings.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Longest palindromic substring
  • Count palindromic substrings
// Example: Longest Palindromic Substring
function expandAroundCenter(s, left, right) {
  while (left >= 0 && right < s.length && s[left] === s[right]) {
    left--;
    right++;
  }
  return right - left - 1;
}

docs.title: 6. Sorting and Comparing
docs.text:
Used when order of characters doesn't matter (e.g., checking if two strings are anagrams).

🔍 Problem Types
  • Group anagrams
  • Sort characters by frequency
// Example: Group Anagrams
let map = new Map();

for (let word of strs) {
  let sorted = word.split("").sort().join("");
  if (!map.has(sorted)) map.set(sorted, []);
  map.get(sorted).push(word);
}

docs.title: 7. Greedy Approach
docs.text:
Used when you want to make optimal choices at each step to build the final result.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Remove K digits
  • Lexicographically smallest string
// Example: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates
let stack = [];

for (let char of s) {
  if (stack.length && stack[stack.length - 1] === char) {
    stack.pop();
  } else {
    stack.push(char);
  }
}
return stack.join("");

docs.title: 8. Dynamic Programming (DP)
docs.text:
Used for overlapping subproblems — like counting substrings, finding longest subsequence, etc.

🔍 Problem Types
  • Longest common subsequence
  • Longest palindromic substring
  • Edit distance
// Example: Longest Common Subsequence
const dp = Array(m + 1)
  .fill()
  .map(() => Array(n + 1).fill(0));

for (let i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
  for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
    if (text1[i - 1] === text2[j - 1]) {
      dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;
    } else {
      dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
    }
  }
}

docs.text:
i have an idea to start my my online project business called assignment tracker where assigment doer can signup and create assigment title and update theier progress. and users can signup and can see their assigment progress and can chat. is there any software like this before research it. and suggest me. refine my ideas

Here’s a refined version of your "Assignment Tracker" concept with clearer differentiators and actionable features to make it stand out in the market:

docs.title: Core Concept Refinement
docs.text: Tagline: “Track assignments, collaborate seamlessly, and deliver results—all in one place.”

docs.title: Key Features to Differentiate Your Platform
1. Dual User Roles
docs.text:
• Assignment Creators (e.g., freelancers, students):

  • Create assignments with titles, deadlines, and detailed descriptions.

  • Upload files (e.g., drafts, research) and update progress via a visual progress bar (e.g., 0–100%).

  • Set milestones (e.g., “Research completed,” “Draft submitted”).

  • Users (e.g., clients, teachers):

  • View real-time progress updates and access uploaded files.

  • Send feedback or comments directly via built-in chat.

docs.title: 2. Integrated Chat System
docs.text:
• Threaded Conversations: Users and creators can discuss assignments in dedicated chat threads.
  • File Sharing: Attach files (e.g., feedback documents, revisions) directly in chats.
  • Notifications: Alerts for new messages, progress updates, or deadlines.

docs.title: 3. Progress Visualization
docs.text:
• Dynamic Dashboard: A centralized view showing all assignments, their status, and deadlines.
  • Customizable Progress Bars: Creators can manually update progress or automate it via integrations (e.g., time-tracking tools).

docs.title: 4. Custom Notifications
docs.text:
• Email/SMS alerts for deadlines, progress updates, or new messages.
  • Priority Flags: Mark urgent assignments for quick visibility.

docs.title: 5. Integration Hub
docs.text:
• File Storage: Sync with Google Drive, Dropbox, or OneDrive for seamless file access.
  • Calendars: Sync deadlines with Google Calendar or Outlook.
  • Third-Party Tools: Integrate with Slack or Discord for broader team communication.

docs.title: Target Audience
docs.text: Group Use Case Freelancers Track client projects, share updates, and collaborate via chat. Students Manage assignments, submit drafts, and receive feedback from teachers. Remote Teams Assign tasks, monitor progress, and discuss deliverables in real time.

docs.title: Monetization Strategies
docs.text:
1. Freemium Model:
    • Free Tier: Basic features (e.g., 3 assignments/month, chat).
    • Premium Tier: Unlimited assignments, advanced integrations, and priority support.
  2. Enterprise Plans: Offer bulk pricing for schools or businesses.
  3. Affiliate Partnerships: Partner with productivity tool providers (e.g., Grammarly, Canva) for cross-promotion.

docs.title: Competitive Edge
docs.text:
• Simplicity: Avoid clutter by focusing on assignment tracking + chat rather than broad project management.
  • Accessibility: Mobile-friendly design for on-the-go updates.
  • Privacy: End-to-end encryption for chats and file sharing.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Assignment Tracker is a web-based platform designed to streamline assignment management and collaboration for freelancers, students, and remote teams. By combining progress tracking, real-time chat, and customizable dashboards, it addresses inefficiencies in current project management tools, offering a user-friendly solution for seamless communication and task oversight.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: Existing tools like Notion or Trello lack integrated chat functionality and dual user roles, forcing users to switch between apps for updates and communication. This fragmentation leads to missed deadlines, miscommunication, and wasted time.

docs.title: Solution Overview
docs.text:
Assignment Tracker solves these issues by:

  1. Simplifying Progress Tracking:

    • Creators (freelancers/students) can set deadlines, upload files, and update progress via a visual progress bar.
    • Users (clients/teachers) view real-time updates and access shared files.

  2. Enabling Real-Time Collaboration:

    • Built-in Chat: Direct messaging for feedback, revisions, or clarifications.
    • File Sharing: Attach documents directly in chat threads.

  3. Enhancing Visibility:

    • Centralized Dashboard: Track all assignments, deadlines, and progress in one place.
    • Notifications: Alerts for updates, deadlines, or messages.

docs.title: Market Opportunity
docs.text:

Group Use Case Freelancers Manage client projects, share updates, and collaborate via chat. Students Track assignments, submit drafts, and receive feedback from teachers. Remote Teams Assign tasks, monitor progress, and discuss deliverables in real time.

docs.title: Application Architecture Overview
docs.text: The architecture will follow a Clean Architecture or N-Layered Architecture approach to ensure scalability, maintainability, and testability. The key layers are:

docs.title: 1. Layers:
docs.text:
1. Presentation Layer (Frontend)

    • Purpose: User interaction and interface.
    • Technologies: React.js, Angular, or Vue.js for a responsive and interactive UI.

    • Features:

      • User dashboards for task tracking and progress visualization.
      • Chat interface with real-time messaging (e.g., WebSocket or SignalR).
      • Role-based access control for assignment creators and viewers.

  2. Application Layer (Backend)

    • Purpose: Business logic and coordination between the frontend and data layer.
    • Technologies: Node.js with Express.js, or ASP.NET Core for robust API development.

    • Features:

      • Task creation, updates, and role-based permissions.
      • Real-time updates using WebSocket or SignalR.
      • Notification services (email/SMS alerts).

  3. Data Layer (Database)

    • Purpose: Persistent storage of assignments, user roles, chat messages, and progress data.

    • Technologies:

      • Relational Database: PostgreSQL or MySQL for structured data (tasks, users).
      • NoSQL Database: MongoDB for unstructured data (chat messages).

  4. Infrastructure Layer

    • Purpose: External integrations and services.
    • Technologies: AWS S3/Google Cloud Storage for file uploads, Firebase for push notifications, and third-party APIs like Google Calendar for deadline syncing.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• Framework: React.js or Vue.js.
  • Tools: TailwindCSS/Bootstrap for styling.

  • Features:

    • Role-based dashboards.
    • Real-time chat using WebSocket.
    • Dynamic progress bars and assignment views.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
• Framework: ASP.NET Core or Node.js with Express.js.

  • Features:

    • RESTful APIs for CRUD operations on tasks.
    • WebSocket/SignalR for real-time updates.
    • Authentication using JWT (JSON Web Tokens).

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
• Relational DB (PostgreSQL/MySQL): Store structured data like users, tasks, roles.
  • NoSQL DB (MongoDB): Store unstructured data like chat logs.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• File Storage: AWS S3/Google Cloud Storage for file uploads.
  • Notification Service: Twilio/Firebase for email/SMS alerts.
  • Integration: APIs for Google Calendar/Slack.

docs.title: 4. Deployment Strategy
docs.text:
Option 1: Monolithic Deployment

  • Deploy all layers as a single unit.
  • Suitable for MVPs or smaller-scale applications.
  • Hosting: Azure App Service or AWS Elastic Beanstalk.

Option 2: Microservices Deployment

  • Split backend services into smaller microservices (e.g., task service, chat service).
  • Suitable for scaling specific features independently.
  • Hosting: Kubernetes/Docker containers on AWS or Azure.

docs.title: 5. Scalability Considerations
docs.text:
• Use a load balancer to distribute traffic across multiple servers.
  • Implement caching (e.g., Redis) to improve response times for frequently accessed data.
  • Use horizontal scaling to handle increased user demand.

This architecture ensures flexibility in development while preparing the platform to scale as your user base grows! Let me know if you need further details on any specific layer or technology choice! 😊

docs.text: Choosing between a web app and a mobile app largely depends on your target audience and market needs. Generally, web apps have a broader reach since they can be accessed on any device with a browser, while mobile apps can offer better performance and user experience on smartphones.

docs.title: Sellable Apps: Web App vs. Mobile App
docs.text:
• Web Apps: Often easier to develop and maintain, they can be updated without user intervention. Ideal for productivity tools, SaaS platforms, and content-heavy applications.
  • Mobile Apps: Tend to have higher engagement and user retention. They are better for apps requiring native device features like GPS, camera, or push notifications. Ideal for social networking, gaming, and lifestyle apps.

The Dashboard page displays the user’s balance using Ant Design’s Card and Statistic components.

// src/pages/Dashboard.js
import React from 'react';
import { useGetUserBalanceQuery } from '../features/apiSlice';
import { Card, Statistic, Spin, Alert } from 'antd';

function Dashboard() {
    const { data: balance, error, isLoading } = useGetUserBalanceQuery();

    if (isLoading) return <Spin />;
    if (error) return <Alert message="Error" description={error.message} type="error" />;

    return (
        <div style={{ padding: 24 }}>
            <Card title="Dashboard" bordered={false} style={{ marginBottom: 16 }}>
                <Statistic title="Total Balance" value={`$${balance?.totalBalance}`} precision={2} />
                <Statistic title="Spending Balance" value={`$${balance?.spendingBalance}`} precision={2} />
            </Card>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Dashboard;

The BalanceManagement page allows users to update their total balance using Ant Design’s Form and InputNumber components.

// src/pages/BalanceManagement.js
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { useGetUserBalanceQuery, useAddSpendingMutation } from '../features/apiSlice';
import { Form, InputNumber, Button, Card, Spin, Alert } from 'antd';

function BalanceManagement() {
    const { data: balance, error, isLoading } = useGetUserBalanceQuery();
    const [updateBalance] = useAddSpendingMutation();
    const [totalBalance, setTotalBalance] = useState(balance?.totalBalance || 0);

    const handleSubmit = async () => {
        try {
            await updateBalance({ totalBalance });
            alert('Balance updated!');
        } catch (err) {
            console.error('Update failed:', err);
        }
    };

    return (
        <div style={{ padding: 24 }}>
            <Card title="Balance Management">
                {isLoading && <Spin />}
                {error && <Alert message="Error" description={error.message} type="error" />}
                {!isLoading && !error && (
                <Form onFinish={handleSubmit}>
                    <Form.Item label="Total Balance">
                        <InputNumber
                            value={totalBalance}
                            onChange={(value) => setTotalBalance(value)}
                            min={0}
                            style={{ width: '100%' }}
                        />
                    </Form.Item>
                    <Form.Item>
                        <Button type="primary" htmlType="submit">Update Balance</Button>
                    </Form.Item>
                </Form>
                )}
            </Card>
        </div>
    );
}

export default BalanceManagement;

The Spending page lists all spending records and includes an option to add a new spending record using Form, InputNumber, and List components from Ant Design.

// src/pages/Spending.js
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { useGetSpendingRecordsQuery, useAddSpendingMutation } from '../features/apiSlice';
import { Form, InputNumber, Button, Card, List, Spin, Alert } from 'antd';

function Spending() {
    const { data: spendingRecords, isLoading, error } = useGetSpendingRecordsQuery();
    const [addSpending] = useAddSpendingMutation();
    const [amount, setAmount] = useState(0);

    const handleAddSpending = async () => {
        try {
            await addSpending({ amount });
            setAmount(0);
            alert('Spending record added!');
        } catch (err) {
            console.error('Add spending failed:', err);
        }
    };

    return (
        <div style={{ padding: 24 }}>
            <Card title="Spending">
                {isLoading && <Spin />}
                {error && <Alert message="Error" description={error.message} type="error" />}

                <Form onFinish={handleAddSpending} layout="inline">
                    <Form.Item label="Amount">
                        <InputNumber
                            value={amount}
                            onChange={(value) => setAmount(value)}
                            min={0}
                        />
                    </Form.Item>
                    <Form.Item>
                        <Button type="primary" htmlType="submit">Add Spending</Button>
                    </Form.Item>
                </Form>

                <List
                    header={<strong>Spending Records</strong>}
                    bordered
                    dataSource={spendingRecords || []}
                    renderItem={(record) => (
                        <List.Item>
                            ${record.amount} - {record.date}
                        </List.Item>
                    )}
                />
            </Card>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Spending;

The Login page uses Ant Design’s Form and Input components.

// src/pages/Login.js
import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { useLoginMutation } from '../features/apiSlice';
import { useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';
import { Form, Input, Button, Card, Alert } from 'antd';

function Login() {
    const [login, { isLoading }] = useLoginMutation();
    const [error, setError] = useState(null);
    const navigate = useNavigate();

    const handleSubmit = async ({ email, password }) => {
        try {
            const { data } = await login({ email, password });
            localStorage.setItem('authToken', data.token);
            navigate('/dashboard');
        } catch (err) {
            setError('Login failed. Please check your credentials.');
        }
    };

    return (
        <div style={{ padding: 24 }}>
            <Card title="Login">
                {error && <Alert message="Error" description={error} type="error" />}

                <Form onFinish={handleSubmit}>
                    <Form.Item name="email" rules={[{ required: true, message: 'Please enter your email!' }]}>
                        <Input placeholder="Email" />
                    </Form.Item>
                    <Form.Item name="password" rules={[{ required: true, message: 'Please enter your password!' }]}>
                        <Input.Password placeholder="Password" />
                    </Form.Item>
                    <Form.Item>
                        <Button type="primary" htmlType="submit" loading={isLoading}>Login</Button>
                    </Form.Item>
                </Form>
            </Card>
        </div>
    );
}

export default Login;
